specPoints.text: understand the methods used to farm large numbers of fish to provide a source of protein, including maintaining water quality, controlling intraspecific and interspecific predation, controlling disease, removing waste products, controlling the quality and frequency of feeding, and selective breeding

primer.text: Fish farming packs protein production into managed water. With wild stocks declining from overfishing, farms control everything from water quality to feeding rhythm. This note tours the methods: filtering water, separating fish by size and species, fighting disease, removing waste, and selective breeding for fast growth.

lessons.title: Why Fish Move to the Farm
lessons.opening: Overfishing has thinned wild populations, so farms raise dense shoals of fish in enclosed freshwater or seawater to supply human protein. Control is the farm's superpower: breeders select fast growers, predators are excluded, water is cleaned, and feeding is timed for growth.
keyPoints: Overfishing has caused dramatic declines in many wild fish populations.
Fish farms rear dense stocks of fish within confined enclosures, supplying protein for human diets.
Selective breeding produces high-quality, fast-growing farmed stock.
Farms protect fish from predators and control water quality, which wild-caught fish cannot promise.
Controlled feeding keeps growth rapid, though the enterprise stays labour-intensive and costly.

low.restatement: Wild fish are getting scarce, so grow them like livestock: safe water, safe pens, good food, best breeders.
low.analogy: A fish city with neighbourhood rules, meal times and a cleanup crew.
low.examPointer: Contrast farm and wild catches by naming mercury pollution as the wild risk.

medium.restatement: Because overfishing has depleted wild stocks, farms rear dense populations in enclosures where breeders select rapid growth, barriers exclude predators, water quality is managed against pollutants such as mercury, and feeding is scheduled to maximise growth — at the cost of labour and expense.
medium.analogy: Trading wild mushroom hunting for a mushroom cellar: less adventure, more certainty per kilogram.
medium.examPointer: When listing advantages, pair each with its wild-caught problem — pollution, unpredictability, predation.

check.stem: What pressure on wild stocks does fish farming help relieve?

options.text: Overfishing has driven dramatic declines in many wild populations
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Wild fish have stopped breeding entirely
options.explanation: Decline, not total collapse, is described.

options.text: Predators have eaten all wild fish
options.explanation: Fishing pressure, not predation, is cited.

options.text: Wild fish migrated to deep trenches
options.explanation: Migration is not the cause named.

check.stem: Which contamination concern does controlled farm water address?

options.text: Wild-caught fish can carry pollutants such as mercury in their flesh
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Farm water adds beneficial mercury
options.explanation: Mercury is the contaminant being avoided.

options.text: Wild fish contain extra vitamins
options.explanation: Vitamins are not the concern raised.

options.text: Salt damages wild fish flesh
options.explanation: Salinity is normal for marine species.

check.stem: How does selective breeding improve a fish farm's output?

options.text: Fish with desired characteristics are allowed to reproduce, passing fast growth on
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: All fish are fed the same regardless of genes
options.explanation: Selection changes which fish breed, not feeding alone.

options.text: Growth hormones are injected weekly
options.explanation: Hormone injection is not the taught method.

options.text: Fish are kept hungry to speed growth
options.explanation: Starvation slows growth.

check.stem: What honest cost of fish farming should a business plan include?

options.text: The enterprise is labour-intensive and costly to run
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Farms need no staff at all
options.explanation: Monitoring fish requires labour.

options.text: Feed is always free from the sea
options.explanation: Feed is bought and managed.

options.text: Profits are guaranteed every season
options.explanation: Costs and risks make profits uncertain.

check.stem: Why do farmed fish grow faster than most wild fish?

options.text: Controlled feeding supplies nutrient-rich food on a frequent schedule
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Farm water is warmer by magic
options.explanation: Any warming is engineered, not magical.

options.text: Wild fish choose to eat less
options.explanation: Wild feeding is opportunistic, not chosen.

options.text: Farmed fish swim less and store fat only
options.explanation: Growth reflects controlled diet, not laziness.

check.stem: State the food role that fish farming fulfils for humans.
check.modelAnswer: Fish farming rears dense stocks of fish in confined enclosures, supplying protein for human diets.

check.stem: Name the breeding technique farms use to improve their stock.
check.modelAnswer: Selective breeding lets farmers breed only fish carrying desired characteristics such as fast growth.

check.stem: Explain why controlling water quality matters more on a farm than at sea.
check.modelAnswer: Farm fish live crowded in one body of water, so waste, low oxygen or disease spread rapidly there, while open water dilutes and disperses such problems.

check.stem: A new farm site has murky, oxygen-poor water. Recommend two fixes before stocking fish.
check.modelAnswer: Install filtration to clear waste and harmful bacteria, and aerate the water so oxygen levels support aerobic respiration in dense stock.

lessons.title: Seven Levers of a High-Yield Farm
sourceHeadings: Methods used in fish farms to ensure high yields
lessons.opening: Every high-yield farm pulls the same seven levers: clean water, separation within the species, barriers between species, disease defence, waste removal, disciplined feeding, and selective breeding. Each lever answers a specific threat that crowded fish would otherwise face.
keyPoints: Water passes through filtration that strips out waste, faeces and harmful bacteria, and cleaning keeps oxygen levels high for aerobic respiration.
Fish are separated by size and age so bigger individuals do not eat or fight smaller ones — controlling intraspecific predation.
Barriers of fences, nets and tanks hold different species apart, preventing interspecific predation and fighting.
Antibiotics prevent disease that close confinement would otherwise spread rapidly, and small groups limit outbreaks.
Feeding uses nutrient-rich food in frequent small amounts so fish grow fast without overeating or turning on each other.
Separating fish by gender lets farmers direct selective breeding so desired characteristics spread through the stock.

low.restatement: Clean water, size-sort the fish, fence off other species, medicate, scoop the waste, feed little and often, breed the best.
low.analogy: Running a boarding school: hygiene, dorm assignments by year group, meal schedules and a nurse on call.
low.examPointer: Use the exact terms intraspecific and interspecific when describing the two predation controls.

medium.restatement: High yields rest on filtration that sustains oxygen and removes bacteria and waste, size-and-age sorting to stop intraspecific predation, physical barriers between species against interspecific predation, antibiotics plus small groupings against disease, frequent nutrient-rich feeding in small portions, and gender separation enabling selective breeding.
medium.analogy: An orchestral score where every section — water, space, health, food, breeding — must stay in time or the concert collapses.
medium.examPointer: Match each method to its threat in the answer: oxygen to respiration, barriers to fighting, antibiotics to confinement disease.

check.stem: Why is water filtered and cleaned continuously on a fish farm?

options.text: To remove waste and harmful bacteria and keep oxygen levels high for aerobic respiration
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: To make the water look clear for visitors
options.explanation: Clarity serves the fish, not tourists.

options.text: To cool the water in summer
options.explanation: Temperature is not the stated purpose.

options.text: To add minerals for faster growth
options.explanation: Mineral dosing is not the filtration goal.

check.stem: What separates intraspecific from interspecific predation?

options.text: Intraspecific occurs within one species, interspecific between different species
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Intraspecific means between species, interspecific within one
options.explanation: The definitions are swapped in that answer.

options.text: Both describe only fights over food
options.explanation: Both are predation or fighting categories.

options.text: Neither occurs among farmed fish
options.explanation: Both drive the separation methods used.

check.stem: How do farms reduce disease spread among crowded fish?

options.text: Antibiotics prevent disease and fish are kept in small numbers to limit outbreaks
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Vaccination of every fish weekly
options.explanation: Antibiotics, not vaccination, is the taught control.

options.text: Letting disease burn out naturally
options.explanation: Confinement would make that dangerous.

options.text: Doubling the feed rate
options.explanation: Extra feed does not treat disease.

check.stem: Why are fish fed frequently but in small amounts?

options.text: So they grow quickly without overeating or attacking each other
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: To save money by wasting less feed
options.explanation: The purpose cited is growth and behaviour.

options.text: Because fish digest food slowly
options.explanation: Digestion speed is not the reason given.

options.text: To keep the water warmer
options.explanation: Feeding has no heating role.

check.stem: A farmer notices larger tank mates chasing smaller ones. Which lever fixes this?

options.text: Separating fish by size and age to stop intraspecific predation
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Adding antibiotics to the water
options.explanation: Antibiotics address disease, not chasing.

options.text: Feeding more nutrients
options.explanation: Feeding helps but separation directly stops the attacks.

options.text: Raising the oxygen level
options.explanation: Oxygen supports respiration, not social order.

check.stem: State two controls that maintain water quality on a fish farm.
check.modelAnswer: Filtration strips waste and harmful bacteria from the water, and cleaning maintains high oxygen for aerobic respiration.

check.stem: Name the two predation types that fish separation controls.
check.modelAnswer: Farms control intraspecific predation within a species and interspecific predation between different species.

check.stem: Explain why disease spreads quickly among farmed fish unless actively controlled.
check.modelAnswer: Close confinement keeps many fish in one volume of water, so a pathogen passes between individuals far faster than in open water, and antibiotics plus small groups slow that spread.

check.stem: Design the weekly routine that keeps a fish farm productive.
check.modelAnswer: Filter and clean the water, check oxygen, separate any mismatched fish by size, dose antibiotics as needed, remove waste, feed nutrient-rich rations little and often, and record which breeders carry the desired characteristics.

glossary.definition: Predation or fighting between members of the same species.
Predation between individuals of different species.
Choosing parents with desired characteristics so the next generation inherits them.
The fenced, netted or tanked water area where farmed fish are kept.
